source.title: Grokking, memorization, and generalization — a discussion

record.file_problem: Full LessWrong discussion and comments are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The authors report their own modular-addition experiments and argue that late generalization after memorization is not universal: in most of their studied architectures generalization improves before training accuracy reaches 50%. They also report optimizer and regularization dependence, refining the scope of the claim.
record.gate_note: The discussion reports qualitative outcomes from the authors’ modular-addition experiments and describes a Fourier-mode visualization. It gives no underlying metrics or full experimental recipe. Statements about results in cited papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The authors report their own modular-addition experiments, run with Nina Rimsky. In most architectures they studied, rapid generalization came before training accuracy reached 50%, and grokking often happened without explicit regularization. Learning rate and optimizer changed whether and how fast generalization occurred. These results argue that V1's late-after-memorization pattern is not universal, and that the weight-decay part of V5 needs qualifying. All evidence is qualitative and self-reported, with no numbers or figure data in the text.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. Additional points the authors make: they use 'grokking' to mean any sudden generalization, whether or not memorization has completed, and find the late-after-memorization form occurs only sometimes. They favor the slingshot/edge-of-stability account for why it is sometimes late. They consider some implicit or explicit low-norm bias probably useful, even though explicit weight decay is usually unnecessary.
record.recipe_differences: An informal discussion reporting modular-addition experiments, not a reproducible account of the original training method; architecture details, dataset sizes, and most hyperparameters are omitted.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that optimizer choice and learning rate change generalization qualitatively and quantitatively, with an architecture- and prime-size-dependent optimal learning rate. The reported effect of explicit regularization also varies by architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam and large learning rates qualitatively favor generalizing over memorizing solutions. Small-lr SGD tends to get stuck in memorization minima. The authors attribute late grokking to slingshot or edge-of-stability effects of stochastic large-lr training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether and when grokking occurs depends on optimizer stochasticity and learning rate: large-lr SGD or Adam favors generalization, and late grokking reflects edge-of-stability dynamics rather than norm regularization alone.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer review not stated
record.problems: Experimental outcomes are self-reported and qualitative, with no numerical metrics, sample sizes, uncertainty estimates, named model configurations, or complete training recipe. The Fourier-mode result is described without numerical plot data. The discussion does not report a training-set-size sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results were omitted. Claims about results from cited papers were excluded because they are not results of this study.

record.verdict_notes: Informal LessWrong dialogue. All experimental claims are qualitative, with no metrics, architectures, primes, dataset sizes or figure data. The study is not an original source for any version. Verdicts should be weighted lightly given the evidence form.

versions.untested_parts: The authors do not report numerical train/test-accuracy curves, chance or near-perfect test accuracy, or a sweep showing how delay changes as training-set size shrinks.

The described Fourier-mode visualization bears on gradual circuit formation, but the discussion does not report that memorizing components are removed later or that continuous progress measures anticipate a test-accuracy jump.
No non-algorithmic datasets or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep is reported.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning experiment is reported.
The authors report effects of regularization, but do not test whether low norm selects a more efficient generalizing circuit or whether a critical dataset size and ungrokking follow.
No comparison of identifiable algorithms across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters is reported.

The authors report optimizer and learning-rate sensitivity, but do not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits in the softmax, nor show that controlling such effects removes the delay.
